content: In the field of chemistry, particularly biochemistry, a fatty acid is defined as a carboxylic acid that typically possesses a long, unbranched aliphatic chain, which can be either saturated or unsaturated. Fatty acids are often synthesized in nature with an even number of carbon atoms due to their biosynthesis involving acetyl-CoA, a coenzyme that carries a two-carbon group. Industrially, fatty acids are produced by hydrolyzing the ester linkages in triglycerides (fats or biological oils), releasing glycerol in the process. Types of Fatty Acids Saturated Fatty Acids Saturated fatty acids lack double bonds or other functional groups along their carbon chain. The term saturated refers to the fact that all carbon atoms, except for the carboxylic acid group, are fully saturated with hydrogen atoms. The omega (ω) end of the chain contains three hydrogens (-CH3), and each internal carbon is bonded to two hydrogens. These fatty acids form straight chains, allowing them to pack tightly together, which facilitates dense energy storage in living organisms. Animal fatty tissues are rich in long-chain saturated fatty acids. In IUPAC nomenclature, fatty acids are named systematically, while common nomenclature often uses the suffix -ic. For example, C18:0 indicates an 18-carbon chain with no double bonds, whereas C18:1 describes an 18-carbon chain with one double bond. The position and configuration (cis or trans) of double bonds can vary, leading to structural diversity among fatty acids. Unsaturated Fatty Acids Unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more double bonds within their carbon chain. These double bonds replace single-bonded -CH2-CH2segments with double-bonded -CH=CHportions. The carbons adjacent to the double bond can adopt either a cis or trans configuration. Most naturally occurring unsaturated fatty acids have cis double bonds and follow a pattern where each double bond is separated by three carbons. The geometric differences between saturated and unsaturated fatty acids, as well as among various unsaturated fatty acids, significantly influence biological processes and the construction of cellular structures, such as membranes. Nomenclature The location of double bonds in fatty acids can be specified using several systems: cis/trans-Delta-x (Δx): Indicates the position of the double bond, counting from the carboxylic acid end. The cis or trans designation specifies the configuration of the double bond. Omega-x (ω-x): Specifies the position of the double bond, counting from the methyl (omega) end of the chain. The symbol ω is sometimes replaced with n, as in n-6 or n-3. IUPAC Nomenclature: A systematic naming system where counting begins from the carboxylic acid end. Cis double bonds are labeled Z, and trans double bonds are labeled E. Examples of Unsaturated Fatty Acids Myristoleic acid is an omega-5 fatty acid. Palmitoleic acid is an omega-7 fatty acid. Oleic acid and erucic acid are omega-9 fatty acids. Stearic acid (C18:0) is a saturated fatty acid, while oleic acid (C18:1) is an unsaturated fatty acid with two fewer hydrogens. Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) are long-chain omega-3 fatty acids found in fish oil. Alpha-linolenic acid is a plant-derived omega-3 fatty acid. Omega-3 fatty acids are associated with health benefits. Linoleic acid and arachidonic acid are omega-6 fatty acids, which may have harmful effects in excess. Essential Fatty Acids The human body can synthesize most fatty acids but cannot produce linoleic acid (LA) and alpha-linolenic acid (LNA), which are essential fatty acids. These are abundant in plant oils. Fish oils provide longer-chain omega-3 fatty acids, such as EPA and DHA, which fulfill essential fatty acid requirements and have additional health benefits. Mammals lack the enzymes to introduce double bonds beyond carbons 9 and 10, making omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids essential in the diet. Essential fatty acids are precursors to hormone-like substances that regulate blood pressure, clotting, lipid levels, immune responses, and inflammation. Imbalances in omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids, common in Western diets, are linked to conditions like depression and behavioral changes, though the exact mechanisms remain under investigation. Trans Fatty Acids Trans fatty acids are unsaturated fatty acids with trans double bonds, which result in a less kinked structure compared to cis double bonds. These are typically produced during industrial hydrogenation of plant oils. Trans fats are associated with an increased risk of circulatory diseases, such as atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease, compared to non-trans fats. Free Fatty Acids Fatty acids can exist in a free state when not bound to other molecules, such as in triglycerides or phospholipids. Free fatty acids are released during the breakdown of triglycerides and serve as an important energy source for tissues, particularly the heart and skeletal muscles. The brain, however, cannot utilize fatty acids for energy and relies on glucose or ketone bodies, which are derived from fatty acid metabolism during starvation or low carbohydrate intake. Fatty Acids in Dietary Fats The composition of fatty acids and cholesterol varies among dietary fats. Longer-chain fatty acids have minimal solubility in water and little effect on solution pH. They can dissolve in warm ethanol and be titrated with sodium hydroxide. The degree of triglyceride hydrolysis can be measured by titration. Reactions of Fatty Acids Fatty acids undergo typical carboxylic acid reactions, including esterification and acid-base reactions. Reduction of fatty acids produces fatty alcohols. Unsaturated fatty acids can participate in addition reactions, such as hydrogenation, which is used to convert vegetable oils into margarine. Partial hydrogenation can isomerize cis double bonds into trans configurations. Certain unsaturated fatty acids can be cleaved in molten alkali, a reaction historically used for structural analysis. Auto-Oxidation and Rancidity At room temperature, fatty acids undergo auto-oxidation, breaking down into hydrocarbons, ketones, aldehydes, epoxides, and alcohols. Trace amounts of heavy metals in fats and oils accelerate this process. Chelating agents, such as citric acid, are often used to mitigate oxidation.
